buildUp: A lens forms the image, so a large zoom lens with many glass elements bends light onto a 36 by 24 mm sensor, with a group of elements that moves to focus.
To control brightness you need an adjustable hole, so a ring of 7 aperture blades closes down inside the lens, which also changes how much of the scene is in focus.
To freeze motion you need a precise timer for light, so a focal-plane shutter with two curtains sits just in front of the sensor.
You want to see through the taking lens, but the sensor is behind it, so a 45-degree mirror bounces the image up to a focusing screen, and a pentaprism flips it the right way round for your eye.
The mirror blocks the sensor's view of focus, so part of it is see-through and a small sub-mirror behind sends light down to a dedicated phase-detection autofocus sensor.

Finally a processor reads millions of pixel counts, builds the picture and saves it to the card, all powered by a battery and held in a stiff magnesium chassis that keeps the lens and sensor perfectly aligned.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Use a lens to form an image, then control how much light reaches the sensor with two knobs: the size of the opening and the length of time it's open. In a DSLR a hinged mirror sends that same image to your eye and to an autofocus sensor while you compose, then flips out of the way for the instant the picture is taken.

hardParts.title: A zoom lens that's sharp everywhere
hardParts.why: Every glass surface bends different colours by different amounts and blurs the edges of the frame, and a zoom has to correct all of that at every focal length from 24 to 70 mm while staying wide open at f/2.8. Designers balance many elements, some with special low-dispersion glass and some with non-spherical surfaces, then build them to tolerances of micrometres.

hardParts.title: A mirror and shutter that move like clockwork
hardParts.why: For each shot the mirror swings up, the shutter curtains race across the sensor in about 3 milliseconds, and the mirror drops and settles again, several times a second for 150,000 shots or more. All of it has to stop dead without bouncing or shaking the camera, or the picture blurs and the viewfinder flickers.

hardParts.title: Focusing in a few milliseconds
hardParts.why: The autofocus sensor must measure focus in dim light, and the lens must then move its focusing glass to within a few micrometres, fast and silently. The sub-mirror must be aligned to a fraction of a degree, or the camera will confidently focus a little in front of or behind your subject.

principles.explanation: Light travels about a third slower in glass than in air, so a ray hitting a curved surface at an angle bends, the way a shopping trolley veers when one wheel hits carpet. A convex lens bends every ray from one point of the scene so they meet again at one point behind it, forming an image. Focusing means moving glass a few millimetres so that meeting point lands on the sensor. Unfortunately different colours bend by different amounts and edges bend differently from the centre, which is why a good zoom needs 15 to 20 pieces of glass correcting each other.
principles.title: Glass bends light to form an image

principles.explanation: Apertures and shutter speeds both come in steps called stops, each of which halves or doubles the light reaching the sensor. The f-number is the focal length divided by the width of the opening. The light let in depends on the opening's area, which grows with the square of its width, so each step of the square root of 2, from f/2.8 to f/4 to f/5.6, halves the light. Photographers call each halving a stop, and shutter speeds use the same steps: 1/250 s lets in half as much light as 1/125 s. From f/2.8 to f/22 is 6 stops, 64 times less light.
principles.title: Stops: doubling and halving light

principles.explanation: Each pixel counts the photons that land on it, and because they arrive randomly, the fewer it catches the noisier the picture, so big pixels and more light make cleaner pictures. When light hits silicon, each photon can knock an electron loose, and each pixel is a bucket collecting those electrons during the exposure. Photons arrive randomly like raindrops, so a count of N comes with a natural wobble of about the square root of N. A pixel catching 10,000 photons is uncertain by about 100, or 1 per cent; one catching 100 is uncertain by 10 per cent, which you see as grainy noise.
principles.title: Pixels count photons

principles.explanation: By comparing the image seen through opposite sides of the lens, the autofocus sensor can tell which way and how far to focus before the lens moves at all. Light passing through the left side of the lens and the right side comes together only when the image is in focus. The autofocus sensor looks at the image through both sides separately: if the two copies line up, it's sharp; if they're shifted apart, the direction of the shift says whether to focus nearer or further and the size says how far. So the lens can jump straight to focus in one move instead of hunting back and forth.
principles.title: Phase detection knows which way to focus

firstPrinciples.problem: Freeze a moment as a sharp picture, whether the scene is lit by moonlight or midday sun, whether it's a still landscape or a bird in flight. You need to gather enough light to avoid a noisy, murky picture, but not so long that anything moving blurs; you need the image sharp exactly where you want it; and you want to see precisely what you'll get before you press the button.

questions.answer: You're looking at the image via the mirror, and the mirror has to flip up out of the way so light can reach the sensor. While it's up, nothing goes to the viewfinder.
questions.question: Why does the viewfinder go black for a moment when you take a picture?

questions.answer: At faster speeds the shutter is only ever a moving slit, so no instant has the whole sensor uncovered. A flash lasts a tiny fraction of that, so it would light only a stripe; at 1/200 s or slower, there's a moment when both curtains are out of the way.
questions.question: Why does a normal flash only work up to about 1/200 s?

questions.answer: The f-number measures the opening's width, but light depends on its area, which goes with the width squared. 2.8 to 4 is a factor of about 1.4 in width, and 1.4 squared is about 2.
questions.question: Going from f/2.8 to f/4 only changes the number a little. Why does it halve the light?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The shutter's fastest speeds are an illusion: its curtains take about 3 milliseconds to cross the sensor, far longer than 1/8000 s. Instead, the second curtain chases the first, leaving a slit about a millimetre wide that sweeps across, so every row of pixels gets exactly 1/8000 s even though the whole sweep takes much longer. A mechanism that's relatively slow ends up timing light with great precision.

name: DSLR Camera
overview:
A camera is a light-tight box with a lens on the front and something light-sensitive at the back. The lens bends light from the scene so it forms a sharp, upside-down image on that surface; in a digital camera it's an image sensor, a chip covered in millions of tiny light-measuring cells, one per pixel.

DSLR stands for digital single-lens reflex. 'Single-lens' means you look through the same lens that takes the picture, and 'reflex' refers to the mirror that makes this possible. A mirror angled at 45 degrees behind the lens bounces the image up onto a focusing screen, and a block of glass called a pentaprism flips it the right way round and sends it out through the viewfinder to your eye. A small secondary mirror sends some light down to the autofocus sensor.

When you press the shutter button, the mirror flips up out of the way, the aperture blades in the lens close to the chosen size, and the shutter's two curtains open and close in a fraction of a second to let light fall on the sensor. The processor reads out millions of measurements, turns them into a picture and saves it to the memory card, all before the mirror drops back down a moment later.

parts.description: Large curved glass element at the front that gathers light from the whole scene.

details.didYouKnow: A zoom like this has roughly 30 or more glass-to-air surfaces; without coatings, over half the light could be lost to reflections before reaching the sensor.
details.howItWorks: The front element bends incoming light inwards so that a wide cone of the scene can be funnelled down the barrel to the groups behind it. Because it is the widest piece of glass, its size largely decides how bright a constant f/2.8 the lens can manage at the long end. Its surfaces carry several layers of anti-reflection coating, and often a slippery outer layer that sheds water, fingerprints and dust.
keyNumbers: Bare glass reflects about 4% of light per surface
details.madeOf: Optical glass ground and polished to a precise curve, then vacuum-coated with very thin layers of metal oxides. The coatings cut the stray reflections that would otherwise wash out contrast and cause flare.

parts.name: Front element

parts.description: Ribbed ring for focusing by hand; it moves the focusing group through gears.

details.didYouKnow: Autofocus lenses use a short focus throw so the motor can travel quickly, which is why old manual-focus lenses, with much longer throws, often feel easier to focus precisely by hand.
details.howItWorks: Turning the ring rotates a geared or friction-coupled drive that nudges the focusing group along its track inside the barrel. On lenses with an ultrasonic ring motor, the coupling lets you grab the ring and override autofocus at any moment without switching modes. A distance scale beside the ring shows roughly where the lens is focused.
keyNumbers: Typically about 90 to 120 degrees of turn from close-up to infinity
details.madeOf: A ribbed rubber sleeve over a plastic or aluminium ring. The rubber gives grip with gloves or wet fingers, and the ribs let you find it by touch while looking through the viewfinder.

parts.name: Focus ring

parts.description: Wide rubber ring that slides the zoom groups apart or together through a cam slot in the barrel.

details.didYouKnow: On some 24 to 70 mm designs the lens is actually at its longest when set to 24 mm and shrinks as you zoom in, the opposite of what most people expect.
details.howItWorks: The zoom ring is fixed to a cam tube with curved slots cut into it. Pins on the moving lens groups ride in these slots, so as the tube turns each group slides forwards or backwards by its own carefully calculated amount. The curves are shaped so the image stays in focus while the focal length changes.
keyNumbers: Typically about 70 to 90 degrees of rotation from 24 to 70 mm
details.madeOf: A wide rubber grip on a plastic or aluminium ring, connected to a cam tube that is usually precision-moulded engineering plastic or machined brass. The cam slots must be accurate to a few hundredths of a millimetre.

parts.name: Zoom ring

parts.description: Outer tube of the lens, with cam slots inside that guide the glass groups as you zoom and focus.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers design zoom lens barrels to be slightly springy so that small knocks flex rather than crack them, which is one reason modern plastic barrels survive drops that would dent metal ones.
details.howItWorks: The barrel is really several tubes nested together: a fixed outer shell, a rotating cam tube and straight guide slots that stop the lens groups from spinning. Together they convert the twist of the rings into precise straight-line movement of the glass. Rubber gaskets at the joints and the mount help keep out dust and drizzle.
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre reinforced polycarbonate or similar engineering plastic for the outer shell, often with aluminium or brass inner parts. Plastic keeps weight down and absorbs knocks, while metal parts hold tight tolerances.

parts.name: Lens barrel

parts.description: Inner tube with sloping slots: as it turns, pins on the glass cells ride along the slots and slide each group by its own amount.

details.didYouKnow: A worn or sandy cam is what makes an old zoom feel gritty. It's also why a dropped lens can go soft on one side: a single bent pin tilts a whole glass group.
details.howItWorks: This tube sits inside the lens with sloping slots cut through its wall. Small pins on each glass cell ride in those slots, so turning the barrel slides the cells along the axis, each by its own amount, depending on the slope of its slot. The slot shapes are worked out so the image stays in focus while the focal length changes.
keyNumbers: Commonly three slots per group, spaced evenly round the tube
Cam pins typically a few millimetres across
Slot accuracy is often within hundredths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Usually engineering plastic or brass and aluminium, with the slots machined or moulded very precisely. Plastic barrels have improved so much that many lenses now use them to save weight, with little loss in accuracy.

parts.name: Cam barrel

parts.description: Light group of lenses that moves a fraction of a millimetre at a time to bring the subject into focus.

details.didYouKnow: Internal focusing means the front of the lens never turns, which matters to anyone using a polarising filter, since its effect depends on the angle it is set at.
details.howItWorks: Instead of moving the whole lens, this design shifts a small, light group of elements inside the barrel, called internal focusing. Moving it slightly changes where the image comes to a point, so the sharpest plane lands exactly on the sensor. Because the group is light and the lens length does not change, the motor can focus fast and the front element does not rotate.
keyNumbers: Moves only a few millimetres over the full focus range
Positioned to within a few micrometres
details.madeOf: Two or three small optical glass elements in a lightweight plastic or aluminium cell. Keeping the group small and light is what lets the focus motor accelerate and stop it so quickly.

parts.name: Focusing group

parts.description: Group of lenses whose spacing changes the focal length from wide-angle to short telephoto.

details.didYouKnow: The first zoom lenses were notoriously soft, and it was only the arrival of computer-aided lens design from the 1960s onwards that let zooms rival fixed lenses for sharpness.
details.howItWorks: A zoom lens has at least two moving groups: one, the variator, changes the overall magnification, while another, the compensator, moves to keep the image focused on the sensor. Changing the spacing between them alters the focal length smoothly from wide-angle to short telephoto. Keeping the maximum aperture at f/2.8 all the way through the range takes careful balancing of these groups.
keyNumbers: Angle of view about 84 degrees at 24 mm
details.madeOf: Optical glass elements held in cells that carry guide pins, usually including low-dispersion glass to stop colour fringes. Several glass types with different properties are combined so their errors cancel.

parts.name: Zoom group

parts.description: Ring motor driven by ultrasonic vibrations: fast, precise and almost silent.

details.didYouKnow: Ultrasonic ring motors began appearing in SLR lenses in the late 1980s, and they were a big reason autofocus became quiet enough for weddings and wildlife.
details.howItWorks: A ring of piezoelectric ceramic is bonded to a toothed metal stator. Applying high-frequency voltage makes the ceramic flex, sending a travelling ripple around the ring, and the tips of the teeth trace tiny ellipses that push the rotor round by friction, like a crowd surfing a person along. Reversing the ripple's direction reverses the motor, and when the power stops friction holds it firmly in place.
keyNumbers: Vibrates at roughly 30 to 40 kHz, above human hearing
Typically focuses in a fraction of a second
details.madeOf: Piezoelectric ceramic bonded to a metal stator, pressed against a metal rotor with a hard-wearing friction layer. The materials must stay stable across temperature so the motor behaves consistently.

parts.name: Ultrasonic focus motor

parts.description: One of seven curved blades that close in to form a smaller hole, controlling how much light gets through.

details.didYouKnow: Bright points of light photographed at small apertures turn into star shapes; with an odd number of blades like seven, each star has twice as many points, so you get 14-pointed stars.
details.howItWorks: The seven blades pivot on pins and are swung inwards together by a ring, forming a roughly circular hole called the diaphragm. While you compose, the lens stays wide open for a bright viewfinder; a split second before exposure, a small motor closes the blades to the chosen setting, then reopens them. Each full f-stop halves the light reaching the sensor.
keyNumbers: Each blade a fraction of a millimetre thick
f/2.8 to f/22 is 6 full stops
details.madeOf: Very thin blackened steel or similar sheet metal, sometimes a carbon-fibre composite. They must be thin, flat, light and non-reflective, and slide over one another without sticking.

parts.name: Aperture blade

parts.description: Ring with a pivot for every blade and a small stepping motor that swings them all inward together when the camera asks.

details.didYouKnow: Out-of-focus highlights take on the shape of the aperture, which is why lens makers curve the blades: a rounder opening gives softer, rounder blur.
details.howItWorks: The ring holds a pivot for each iris blade, and a small stepping motor turns a second ring that swings them all inward together. The camera body sends the size it wants over the mount's contacts, the lens's own electronics count the motor's steps, and the opening shrinks just before the shutter fires.
keyNumbers: Each full stop halves the light
Stops down in a small fraction of a second
details.madeOf: Thin blackened steel for the blades, with plastic or metal rings, and a small stepper motor with copper windings. The blackening stops light scattering off the blades.

parts.name: Aperture mechanism

parts.description: Small curved circuit board that talks to the camera through the mount and drives the lens's motors.

details.didYouKnow: Because the lens tells the body its exact optical faults, cameras can fix distortion and colour fringing automatically, and some lenses are deliberately designed to rely on that.
details.howItWorks: A modern lens is a small computer. This curved board talks to the camera through the gold contacts, drives the focus motor and aperture, reads where the zoom and focus groups sit, and tells the body exactly which lens is attached so it can correct the picture.
keyNumbers: Usually around a dozen or fewer contacts at the mount
Holds correction data for its own optics
details.madeOf: A thin glass-fibre circuit board cut to a crescent to fit round the light path, with flexible ribbon cables out to the motor, encoders and contacts.

parts.name: Lens circuit board

parts.description: Last glass group, which sharpens the image across the whole frame before it leaves the lens.

details.didYouKnow: Digital sensors are fussier than film about light arriving at a steep angle, because each pixel sits at the bottom of a tiny well, so lenses designed for digital pay extra attention to their rear group.
details.howItWorks: The rear group corrects the last remaining aberrations and shapes how the light leaves the lens so it strikes the sensor at a comfortable angle, even at the corners. Elements here are often aspherical, meaning their curve is not part of a perfect sphere, which helps keep edges sharp without adding extra glass. It sits just in front of the mount, a short distance from the mirror.
keyNumbers: Arranged in about a dozen groups
Usually 2 to 4 aspherical surfaces in the design
details.madeOf: Optical glass, often including aspherical elements that are precision-moulded or ground. Across the whole lens there are typically 15 to 20 elements, some made of low-dispersion glass to tame colour fringing.

parts.name: Rear element group

parts.description: Bayonet ring of chrome-plated brass: twist the lens and it locks in, with gold contacts carrying power and data.

details.didYouKnow: Some SLR lens mounts have stayed largely unchanged for over 60 years, so certain lenses made in the 1960s can still be fitted to modern digital bodies.
details.howItWorks: The mount's lugs slip past matching lugs on the camera, and a short twist slides them under spring-loaded tabs until a locking pin clicks into a hole. This sets the lens at an exact distance from the sensor, called the flange distance, which the lens designers relied on. Spring-loaded gold contacts pass power to the focus motor and let the lens tell the camera its focal length, aperture and focus distance.
keyNumbers: Flange distance typically about 44 to 47 mm
Locks with a twist of roughly 60 to 90 degrees
details.madeOf: Chrome-plated brass or stainless steel, chosen because it wears very slowly over thousands of lens changes and stays dimensionally accurate. The contacts are gold-plated so they resist corrosion.

parts.name: Lens mount

parts.description: Half-silvered mirror at 45° that reflects the image up into the viewfinder and flips up when you take a picture.

details.didYouKnow: Early SLRs left the mirror up after each shot, blacking out the viewfinder until you wound on; the instant-return mirror that drops straight back arrived in the 1950s.
details.howItWorks: Most of the light is bounced upwards onto the focusing screen, but a central patch is only partly silvered so some light passes through to the sub-mirror behind. When you press the shutter, a spring and motor swing the mirror up out of the way in milliseconds, the shutter fires, and the mirror drops back down. Dampers stop it bouncing so the camera shakes less and the viewfinder returns quickly.
keyNumbers: Sits at 45 degrees to the light path
Flips up and back roughly 6 to 10 times per second in burst shooting
Centre passes roughly a third of the light
details.madeOf: Thin glass silvered on its front surface rather than the back, so the image is not doubled by reflections inside the glass. The coating is delicate and should never be wiped.

parts.name: Main mirror

parts.description: Small mirror behind the main one that sends light down to the autofocus sensor.

details.didYouKnow: Because autofocus uses a different light path from the image itself, a DSLR can consistently focus slightly in front of or behind the subject; that is why many cameras offer a per-lens autofocus fine-tune setting.
details.howItWorks: Hinged to the back of the main mirror, the sub-mirror catches the light passing through its semi-transparent centre and angles it down into the autofocus module in the floor of the mirror box. When the main mirror flips up, the sub-mirror folds flat against it so both clear the light path together. Its angle must be precise or autofocus will be slightly off.
keyNumbers: Typically just a few centimetres across
Alignment set to a fraction of a degree
details.madeOf: A small piece of front-silvered glass or coated metal on a light hinged frame. It must be very flat and very light so it can move with the main mirror without bouncing.

parts.name: Sub-mirror

parts.description: Phase-detection module in the floor of the mirror box that works out which way and how far to focus.

details.didYouKnow: Phase-detection autofocus built into an SLR body became a mass-market success in 1985, and within a few years almost every new SLR had it.
details.howItWorks: Small separator lenses split the light from each side of the lens into two images that fall on rows of light sensors. When the subject is in focus the two images line up in a set position; if not, the gap between them tells the camera both which direction and how far to drive the lens. This lets it focus in one decisive move instead of hunting back and forth.
keyNumbers: Works down to about -3 EV, near moonlight
Measures focus in a few milliseconds
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic housing containing tiny separator lenses, masks and CMOS line sensors on a small circuit board. Plastic optics keep it compact and light.

parts.name: Autofocus sensor

parts.description: Light-tight chamber behind the mount that houses the mirrors and their flipping mechanism.

details.didYouKnow: The deep mirror box is the main reason SLRs are bulkier than mirrorless cameras, whose lenses can sit much closer to the sensor.
details.howItWorks: The mirror box sits between the lens mount and the shutter and holds the hinged mirrors, their springs, dampers and the motor-driven cams that raise and lower them. Its walls are blackened and often ribbed to stop stray light bouncing around and fogging the image. It also fixes the exact geometry between lens, mirror, screen and sensor.
keyNumbers: Depth roughly 40 mm, set by the flange distance
Light-tight to stray light from all sides
details.madeOf: Die-cast aluminium or magnesium alloy, or a stiff engineering plastic bolted to the chassis, finished in matt black with light-trapping ridges. It must be rigid so the mirror lands in exactly the same place every time.

parts.name: Mirror box

parts.description: Small motor, gears and spring on the side of the mirror box that flip the mirror up for each shot and bring it back down.

details.didYouKnow: Mirror slap, the shudder when the mirror hits its stop, can blur long exposures, which is why many cameras offer a mode that lifts the mirror first and waits before opening the shutter.
details.howItWorks: A small motor winds a train of gears that turns a cam. On each shot the cam lets a spring snap the mirror up out of the light path, and then the motor brings it back down and resets the spring for the next frame. All of it has to happen in a small fraction of a second, and the mirror must stop without bouncing or the viewfinder and autofocus would be disturbed.
keyNumbers: Fast cameras cycle the mirror many times a second
Often rated with the shutter for a hundred thousand or more shots
details.madeOf: A coreless or brushed DC motor, brass and plastic gears, spring steel and a metal mounting plate, often with small rubber or air dampers to soften the mirror's landing.

parts.name: Mirror drive

parts.description: Frosted screen above the mirror where the image forms, with the focus points etched on it.

details.didYouKnow: Bright modern screens make it hard to judge depth of field at wide apertures, because they can hide how shallow focus really is below about f/2.8.
details.howItWorks: The main mirror projects the image onto this screen, which sits at exactly the same optical distance as the sensor, so what looks sharp here will be sharp in the photo. A fine matt surface makes the image visible, and a Fresnel lens pattern on the other face redirects light from the edges towards your eye so the corners are not dim. Above it, the pentaprism carries the image to the eyepiece.
keyNumbers: About 36 by 24 mm, matching the sensor
Fresnel ridges a fraction of a millimetre apart
details.madeOf: Precision-moulded acrylic or glass with a microscopically textured surface. Many modern screens also include a thin transparent LCD layer that can light up focus points and grid lines.

parts.name: Focusing screen

parts.description: Five-sided block of glass with silvered faces that turns the upside-down, back-to-front image the right way round.

details.didYouKnow: Eye-level pentaprism viewfinders first appeared on SLRs around 1949; before that, you looked down into the camera at a reversed image on a screen.
details.howItWorks: The image on the focusing screen is upside down and reversed left to right. Light entering the prism reflects off a roof-shaped pair of faces and another silvered face, which flips it both ways so you see the scene exactly as it is. Next to the prism sits a metering sensor that reads light from the screen to set exposure and help recognise subjects.
details.madeOf: A solid block of optical glass with silvered or aluminised faces. Cheaper cameras use a lighter, hollow pentamirror of three mirrors, which gives a dimmer view.

parts.name: Pentaprism

parts.description: Lens and rubber eyecup at the back that you look through.

details.didYouKnow: Light leaking in through an uncovered eyepiece can fool the meter during long tripod exposures, which is why many cameras include a small eyepiece cover or shutter.
details.howItWorks: The eyepiece lens magnifies the image coming out of the pentaprism so it looks large and sharp to your eye. A small dial moves an element to adjust the dioptre, letting glasses-wearers and others set the view sharp without their spectacles. The rubber eyecup blocks stray light and cushions your face and glasses.
keyNumbers: Eyepoint around 20 mm from the lens
details.madeOf: Small glass or acrylic lenses in a plastic housing, surrounded by a soft rubber eyecup. Rubber is comfortable, grippy and easy to replace when it wears out.

parts.name: Viewfinder eyepiece

parts.description: Two curtains of thin blades that sweep across the sensor: the gap between them sets the exposure time.

details.didYouKnow: Shutters travel vertically across the short 24 mm side of the frame rather than the long 36 mm side, because the shorter trip lets the curtains finish crossing sooner.
details.howItWorks: When you press the button, the first curtain drops to uncover the sensor and a set time later the second curtain follows to cover it again. At slow speeds the whole frame is open at once, but at fast speeds the second curtain starts before the first has finished, so a narrow slit sweeps across the sensor. A flash fires in an instant, so it only lights the whole frame at speeds slow enough for the sensor to be fully open.
keyNumbers: Each curtain crosses in roughly 3 milliseconds
details.madeOf: Very thin blades of aluminium alloy, titanium or carbon-fibre composite, driven by springs and electromagnets. The blades must be extremely light to start and stop so fast without wearing out.

parts.name: Focal-plane shutter

parts.description: Full-frame chip, 36 × 24 mm, covered in about 24 million light-sensitive cells under a grid of tiny colour filters.

details.didYouKnow: The colour filter grid has twice as many green filters as red or blue, mimicking the human eye's extra sensitivity to green; it was patented by Kodak engineer Bryce Bayer in 1976.
details.howItWorks: Each photosite collects light during the exposure and turns it into an electric charge proportional to brightness. A tiny microlens over each one focuses light into it, and a colour filter means each records only red, green or blue. The camera then estimates the two missing colours at every pixel from its neighbours. In front sits a stack of filters that block infrared and often vibrate to shake off dust.
keyNumbers: Up to about 14 stops of dynamic range
details.madeOf: A CMOS chip made from a thin wafer of silicon, with millions of photodiodes and transistors etched into it, topped with dyed colour filters and microlenses. Silicon naturally releases electrons when struck by visible light.

parts.name: Image sensor

parts.description: Circuit board carrying the sensor and the chips that read out and digitise its signal.

details.didYouKnow: If the sensor is tilted even slightly relative to the mount, one side of the frame will be softer than the other, so factories align it with lasers or test charts.
details.howItWorks: This board holds the sensor exactly parallel to the lens mount and supplies it with clean, stable power. Analogue-to-digital converters, often built into the sensor itself, turn each pixel's charge into a number and stream millions of values per frame to the main board through a fine ribbon cable. Any electrical noise here would show up as speckle in the picture.
keyNumbers: Typically 14-bit conversion, about 16,000 brightness levels per pixel
Reads roughly 24 million pixels per frame
Sensor aligned to within a few hundredths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: A multi-layer fibreglass circuit board with copper tracks, mounted on a metal plate that also spreads heat. The plate is shimmed or adjusted so the sensor sits perfectly square to the lens.

parts.name: Sensor board

parts.description: The camera's computer: processes each picture, runs autofocus and metering, and writes files to the card.

details.didYouKnow: One of the earliest digital cameras, built in a lab in 1975, took about 23 seconds to record a single 0.01-megapixel black-and-white image onto cassette tape.
details.howItWorks: A dedicated image processor turns the raw sensor data into a photo: it fills in the missing colours, sets white balance, reduces noise, sharpens and compresses the result to JPEG. At the same time it reads the autofocus and metering sensors, drives the lens, fires the shutter and runs the menus. Fast memory acts as a buffer so you can keep shooting while earlier frames are still being written to the card.
keyNumbers: Raw files roughly 25 to 45 MB each
Bursts of about 6 to 10 frames per second
details.madeOf: A multi-layer printed circuit board carrying the image processor chip, memory, power regulators and connectors. Many layers are needed to route thousands of fast signals in a small space.

parts.name: Main processor board

parts.description: Rechargeable lithium-ion pack in the grip, good for several hundred to around a thousand shots per charge.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when stored fully charged and warm, so for long storage it is best to keep them about half full somewhere cool.
details.howItWorks: Two lithium-ion cells in series supply about 7.2 volts, which regulators convert to the various voltages the electronics, motors and screen need. A small chip in the pack reports its charge level and temperature to the camera. Because an optical viewfinder needs no power, DSLRs typically get far more shots per charge than cameras that keep a screen running.
keyNumbers: Several hundred to over a thousand shots per charge
details.madeOf: Lithium-ion cells with a protection circuit, sealed in a tough plastic case with metal contacts. Lithium-ion stores a lot of energy for its weight and does not need to be fully run down before recharging.

parts.name: Battery

parts.description: Flash memory card in a slot in the grip that stores the pictures.

details.didYouKnow: The little lock switch on the side of an SD card does nothing electrically to the card; it is simply read by the camera, which then politely refuses to write.
details.howItWorks: Pictures are written into NAND flash memory, where each bit is stored as electric charge trapped on a tiny insulated gate that keeps it even without power. A small controller chip on the card spreads writes across the memory so no area wears out early. The card's write speed decides how quickly the camera's buffer can empty during a burst.
keyNumbers: Write speeds of roughly 30 to 250 MB per second
Holds roughly 2,000 to 8,000 raw files at 128 GB
details.madeOf: Flash memory and a controller chip on a tiny circuit board inside a moulded plastic shell with metal contacts. The plastic keeps it light and cheap while protecting the chips.

parts.name: Memory card

parts.description: 3-inch LCD for reviewing pictures and menus, with a toughened cover glass.

details.didYouKnow: Screen resolution is quoted in dots, and each full-colour pixel uses three of them, so a screen of about a million dots really has around 350,000 pixels.
details.howItWorks: The LCD shows pictures after they are taken, menus and settings, and in live view a feed straight from the sensor with the mirror locked up. A backlight shines through layers of liquid crystal and colour filters, and each dot blocks or passes light to build the image. Some screens are also touch-sensitive and can tilt on a hinge for high or low shots.
details.madeOf: A thin-film transistor LCD panel with LED backlight, protected by a toughened cover glass or hard-coated resin. The cover resists scratches and can be bonded to the panel to reduce reflections.

parts.name: Rear screen

parts.description: Back panel of the body with the buttons, joystick and screen hinge.

details.didYouKnow: Buttons on weather-sealed cameras sit on flexible rubber membranes, so the switch underneath is never exposed even while you press it.
details.howItWorks: The rear cover carries the menu buttons, a joystick for picking focus points and the screen with its hinge, each wired to the main board by flexible ribbon cables. Rubber gaskets around every button and seam help keep out dust and moisture. Its layout is designed so most controls fall under the right thumb while your eye stays at the viewfinder.
details.madeOf: Magnesium alloy or tough polycarbonate, with rubber button covers and seals. Plastic keeps weight and cost down; magnesium adds stiffness on tougher models.

parts.name: Rear cover

parts.description: Die-cast magnesium-alloy frame everything bolts to; light, stiff and sealed against dust and drizzle.

details.didYouKnow: Thixomoulding injects magnesium alloy in a semi-solid, slushy state, a bit like plastic injection moulding, which allows thinner, more detailed parts than ordinary casting.
details.howItWorks: The chassis is the camera's skeleton: the lens mount, mirror box, shutter, sensor and tripod socket all bolt to it, so it sets the precise alignment between them. It also carries the weight of heavy lenses hanging off the front and spreads knocks so delicate parts stay aligned. Body panels and seals fix onto it to make the shell.
keyNumbers: Magnesium is about a third lighter than aluminium
Body typically 750 to 900 g with battery
details.madeOf: Die-cast or thixomoulded magnesium alloy, the lightest structural metal in common use. It is stiff, absorbs vibration well and helps conduct heat away from the sensor.

parts.name: Magnesium chassis

parts.description: Front skin of the body around the lens mount, covered in grippy textured rubber.

details.didYouKnow: The depth-of-field preview button closes the aperture to the chosen setting so you can see how much will be sharp, since the viewfinder normally shows the lens wide open.
details.howItWorks: The front cover wraps around the lens mount and holds the lens release button, a depth-of-field preview button and usually an autofocus assist lamp. Its textured rubber gives your left hand and fingers a secure hold. Behind it, the mount bolts through to the chassis rather than relying on the cover for strength.
keyNumbers: Lens release button typically 1 to 1.5 cm across
details.madeOf: Magnesium alloy or engineering plastic covered in textured synthetic rubber. The rubber is glued in panels and can be replaced if it starts to peel.

parts.name: Front cover

parts.description: Deep rubber-covered grip on the right that houses the battery and card slot.

details.didYouKnow: A deep grip is a big part of why DSLRs feel comfortable with heavy lenses, because it lets you hold the weight with your fingers rather than squeezing with your thumb.
details.howItWorks: The grip gives your right hand a firm hold, with fingers wrapped round the front and the thumb resting on the back. Its bulk makes room for the battery compartment and the card slot behind a sealed door. Many grips also have a front dial and an infrared remote receiver.
keyNumbers: Supports a camera and lens of roughly 1.5 to 2 kg
details.madeOf: A magnesium or plastic shell covered in soft textured rubber. The rubber's slight give and friction help you hold a heavy camera and lens steady.

parts.name: Hand grip

parts.description: Hump on top that covers the pentaprism, with the hot shoe and pop-up flash.

details.didYouKnow: Many professional full-frame cameras leave out the pop-up flash entirely, partly to make room for a larger prism and partly to improve weather sealing.
details.howItWorks: The hump covers the pentaprism, the metering sensor and the eyepiece optics, and supports the hot shoe on top. A small pop-up flash sits on hinges inside it and springs up when needed, raising the light above the lens to reduce red-eye and lens shadows. The top plate also carries the mode dial and a small status display on many models.
keyNumbers: Pop-up flash guide number about 12 m at ISO 100
Flash raised roughly 2 to 3 cm above the body
Flash recycles in a few seconds
details.madeOf: Magnesium alloy or plastic; plastic is often used on top because metal would block the radio signals from built-in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or GPS antennas.

parts.name: Prism housing & top plate

parts.description: Metal bracket with electrical contacts for attaching an external flash.

details.didYouKnow: It is called a hot shoe because it carries electrical contacts; the plain clip it replaced, used just to hold accessories, is known as a cold shoe.
details.howItWorks: An external flash slides into the rails and locks in place. The large centre contact tells the flash to fire at the moment the shutter is fully open, while smaller extra contacts let camera and flash talk, setting flash power automatically from a quick pre-flash. It can also trigger wireless controllers for off-camera lights.
keyNumbers: Pre-flash measured in a few milliseconds
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or aluminium rails with gold-plated contacts set in an insulating plastic base. Metal rails take repeated sliding and the weight of a heavy flash.

parts.name: Hot shoe

parts.description: Dial for choosing automatic, priority or fully manual exposure modes.

details.didYouKnow: The labels Av and Tv on some cameras stand for aperture value and time value, terms from an exposure system devised in the 1960s to make exposure maths easier.
details.howItWorks: The dial tells the camera how much of the exposure to decide for you. In program mode it picks both shutter speed and aperture; in aperture priority you set the aperture and it chooses the speed; in shutter priority the reverse; and in manual you set both. Clicks, called detents, hold each position, and a lock button often stops it being knocked.
keyNumbers: Each position a click of roughly 30 to 40 degrees
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic or aluminium with printed or engraved markings, sitting on a rotary switch. A knurled edge makes it easy to turn with a fingertip.

parts.name: Mode dial

parts.description: Two-stage button: half-press to focus and meter, full press to take the picture.

details.didYouKnow: Many older film cameras had a threaded hole in the middle of the shutter button for a mechanical cable release, a design still found on a few cameras today.
details.howItWorks: Inside are two switches stacked one above the other. A light half-press closes the first, waking the camera to meter and focus; pressing further closes the second, which starts the mirror, aperture and shutter sequence. The two-stage feel lets you lock focus and then recompose before taking the shot.
keyNumbers: Shutter lag as little as about 50 milliseconds
details.madeOf: A metal or plastic cap over two small dome or leaf switches. Metal gives a solid feel and resists wear from hundreds of thousands of presses.

parts.name: Shutter button

parts.description: Thumb wheel by the shutter button for changing shutter speed or aperture.

details.didYouKnow: The same two-pulse encoder trick is used in computer mouse scroll wheels and car volume knobs to tell which way they are being turned.
details.howItWorks: The wheel drives a rotary encoder that produces two slightly out-of-step pulses as it turns; the camera checks which comes first to tell which direction you are spinning. Each click typically changes shutter speed or aperture by a third of a stop. Its job changes with the mode dial, so in manual it might set the speed while a second dial sets the aperture.
keyNumbers: Shutter speeds from about 30 s to 1/8000 s, around 18 stops
details.madeOf: A ridged plastic or rubber-covered wheel on a small electronic encoder. The ridges and clicky detents let you count changes by feel without looking.

parts.name: Command dial

summary: A full-frame digital SLR with a 24–70 mm zoom lens: a flip-up mirror and glass prism show you exactly what the lens sees, until the shutter opens and a 24-megapixel sensor records the picture.
